_what: Hypotheses are this map's own reasoning about where infiltration is likely and unrecorded. They are not cases, they carry no evidence, and nothing in them should be read as a finding about any named person. Each one states the rule that produced it, the conditions it rests on, what the map already documents nearby, and what would show or refute it. They are displayed apart from the patterns for that reason.

items.title: Seventeen countries where insiders are rated severe and this map holds almost nothing
items.claim: In these countries the gap is in cases of this shape - an outside party reaching in - and not necessarily in prosecutions, which some of them bring and win for conduct this map's test excludes.
items.rule: Countries the Global Organized Crime Index scores 7.5 or higher for state-embedded actors - people inside the government, police, courts and army working with or for criminal groups - where this map holds two cases or fewer. The index scores all 193 UN member states with the same questions, so the comparison does not come from this map's own sample.
items.conditions: Across the whole index, countries scoring between 8 and 9 hold a median of 6 cases on this map and those scoring 9 or more hold a median of 2.5, against a median of 2 for the countries in the 6-to-7 band. The seventeen below sit at the top of the index and at the bottom of the record. Checked against outside sources on 14 November 2026, the claim about the record holds and the reason for it is not the same everywhere: Jamaica's courts do bring and win corruption cases against customs officers, a police superintendent and, in 2025 and 2026, officers of the firearms and counter-terrorism branches - but an officer soliciting money from a passenger or extorting a suspect is an official enriching himself, which BRIEF11 excludes as incidental. So for at least one of the seventeen the prosecutions exist and the test filters them out.
items.documented: What these countries do have is usually a single foreign prosecution: Turkmenistan is on the map because German prosecutors charged a MAN manager, Congo-Brazzaville because Swiss prosecutors fined Gunvor, Cameroon because of Glencore. None of the seventeen is on the map through a case its own courts brought.
items.would_show: A prosecution, commission, leak or sustained piece of reporting naming an outside party, a body and a decision. An agent sent to one of these countries should look for the outside party first, not for corruption prosecutions in general, which may be plentiful and still yield nothing.
items.would_refute: A serious published attempt to look that found little. Cabo Verde is the example of the other outcome: the index scores its insiders low and its courts comparatively strong, and the map's writeup says so rather than assuming concealment.

items.title: Companies are reached far more often than this map can show
items.claim: Infiltration of companies is the biggest single hole in the record, and the shortfall is in the record rather than in the world.
items.rule: The case file holds 209 of 1,680 cases - 12 per cent - where the body reached is a company, including state-owned ones. The map's own estimate of the worldwide field, which is not scaled from its sample, puts that share at about 30 per cent. Closing the gap by addition alone would take roughly 420 more cases of that kind.
items.conditions: The same comparison puts companies and industry as the infiltrator at 32 per cent of the map against an estimated 45, and crime groups at 25 against 30. Governments and spy services are the other way round: foreign states are 24 per cent of the map against an estimated 10.
items.documented: The kinds the map does hold show what the missing cases look like: a state oil company's officers paid by a trader, a bank relationship manager moving a trafficking group's money, a terminal operator's staff opening containers, a purchasing manager taking a commission.
items.would_show: Company cases surface through regulators, debarment lists, employment tribunals and internal investigations rather than criminal courts. The test is whether those sources, worked systematically, yield cases at the rate the estimate implies. Two limits measured on 14 November 2026 say the yield per document read will be lower than the top of any list suggests: an enforcement action is not a case - a books-and-records-only action names no body and no decision and fails ruling 11, as SQM in Chile did on re-checking - and the map already matches the largest actions, so what is left in the American corpus is its smaller and older end. Stanford's clearinghouse puts the ten-year average at 36 enforcement actions a year, which is a corpus of several hundred, almost all of it post-2010; the shortfall needs the other seams in BRIEF16 as well.
items.would_refute: Working them and finding the record genuinely thin, which would mean the estimate is too high rather than the map too empty.

items.title: Nine company sanctions whose facts the state has withheld
items.claim: Nine entries on the benchmark lists are convictions or settlements in which the authority named no company and no official, so infiltration is established and cannot be placed.
items.rule: Benchmark items with no matching case where the recorded reason is anonymisation by the authority: four in Germany, where the Länder anonymise case data and the report attributes it to national and constitutional data-protection rules; four in Switzerland, where the Office of the Attorney General named the company in six of its ten summary penalty orders and not in the other four; and one in the Netherlands, the Nabburg settlement.
items.conditions: These are not gaps in research. The German report says the anonymisation made it hard for the OECD's own evaluators to reconcile the cases with what the press had alleged.
items.documented: The grounds are on the record even where the subjects are not. Three of the four German entries are the bribery of foreign officials under sections 334 and 335 of the criminal code, one of them a construction company and its joint-venture partner in Hesse, and the fourth is a failure to supervise whose underlying payments the annex does not describe. All four Swiss entries are the bribery of foreign officials under article 322septies, with compensatory claims running from 73,346 francs to 37 million.
items.would_show: A later court file, a parliamentary question, or a reconstruction from the fine's size and date.
items.would_refute: Nothing refutes it. These are findings whose subjects the state has sealed, which is why they sit here rather than in the gaps.

items.title: National oil and gas companies that an outside party has reached, where nobody has looked
items.claim: Where a state company sells the oil or gas and the officials around it are rated severe, an outside party has probably reached inside it - a trader buying the award, or a security service taking the company over - and in some producers nothing has been published either way.
items.rule: The map documents an outside party inside a state or national oil company in 25 countries and 55 cases - Sonangol, Petrobras, Pemex, PDVSA, NNPC, SNPC, GEPetrol, Turkmennebit and Intergas Central Asia among them. The candidates are producers that sell through a state company, score 7.5 or higher for insiders, and carry no case about that company here. The hypothesis originally looked only for traders; tested against outside sources on 14 November 2026 it was too narrow, and is widened to any outside party.
items.conditions: Gabon scores 7.5 and holds two cases, neither about Gabon Oil Company. South Sudan scores 9.0 and - until this round - held two, neither about Nilepet. Both sell crude through a state company into the same trading houses convicted elsewhere.
items.documented: The widening came from finding what the narrow version would have missed. South Sudan's case is not a trader at all: the United Nations Panel of Experts found the Internal Security Bureau's director general on Nilepet's board and the service's agents among its staff, and that is now on the map. Gabon's richest-looking material fails for a reason already settled: the Gabon Oil Company convictions of July 2022 are embezzlement from the company's own funds, with no outside party, which is the ground on which an earlier round closed Elf/Gabon. What Gabon does have is open and thin - Swiss prosecutors raided Gunvor's Geneva offices in 2026 over a 2024 deal, against persons unknown, with no official named.
items.would_show: A prosecution or settlement in a buyer's home jurisdiction naming the state company, which is how almost every comparable case arrived; or a United Nations panel, commission or sanctions finding on who sits on the board and whose bills the company pays.
items.would_refute: A credible audit of the award process in one of these producers finding it clean.

items.title: Container terminals and customs posts on the cocaine routes
items.claim: At the large transshipment ports where nothing is documented, the terminal and customs staff are probably being recruited in the way they demonstrably are at Antwerp and Saint Petersburg.
items.rule: The map records customs or border officials reached in 45 countries, 60 cases, and terminal or port workers in a handful of those. Where the container volume on a known route is large and the record is empty, the absence is the thing that needs explaining.
items.conditions: The documented instances cluster where a police service published: Belgian federal police on Antwerp port workers, police and customs; Spanish investigations in the Campo de Gibraltar; Bulgarian customs and border officials; a Kyrgyz customs deputy chief; German prosecutors on Saint Petersburg through a Deutsche Bahn subsidiary.
items.documented: The mechanism is consistent wherever it has been examined: a reference inside the terminal to release a container, or a customs officer to wave it through, bought for a fraction of the cargo's value.
items.would_show: A national police or prosecutor's report naming a terminal, a shift or a customs post.
items.would_refute: A port where the containers move on the route and a serious investigation finds no insider, which has not yet been reported anywhere.

items.title: Mining licence offices, which are barely on the record at all
items.claim: The offices that award mining rights are probably reached as often as the ones that award oil cargoes, and the map holds almost nothing on them.
items.rule: Four cases on the whole map turn on mining rights, a mining code or a land cadastre - Guinea, the Central African Republic, India and one Ukrainian land-registry case - against 55 cases touching a state or national oil company across 25 countries. Minerals are awarded by licence in dozens of countries whose insiders the index scores severe.
items.conditions: The imbalance is unlikely to be real. A mining licence is a single signature on an asset worth hundreds of millions, which is the same shape as the oil cases, and the few documented instances reach the top: Guinea's president's wife, and in the Central African Republic a report that Wagner's firms shaped the mining code itself.
items.documented: What the record does hold is mostly the buyer's end - Glencore's purchase of stakes from the Congolese state mining company, Steinmetz in Guinea - rather than the licensing office.
items.would_show: An extractive-industries audit, a licence review by an incoming government, or a debarment naming the cadastre.
items.would_refute: Licence reviews in several high-scoring producers finding the registers sound.
